title: Predicting Bald Eagle Collision at Wind Energy Facilities
abstract: Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) are currently protected in the United States under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act of 1940 and Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918. Given these protections and the increasing development of wind energy throughout the United States, it is important for regulators and the wind industry to understand the risk of bald eagle collisions with wind turbines. Prior probability distributions for eagle exposure rates and collision rates have been developed for golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). Given similar information has not been available for bald eagles, the current recommendation by the USFWS is to use the prior probability distributions developed using data collected on golden eagles to predict take for bald eagles. But some evidence suggests that bald and golden eagles may be at different risk for collision with wind turbines and the prior probability distributions developed for golden eagles may not be appropriate for bald eagles. We developed prior probability distributions using data collected at MidAmerican Energy Company's operating wind energy facilities in Iowa, USA, from December 2014 to March 2017 for bald eagle exposure rates and collision rates. The prior probability distribution for collision rate developed for bald eagles has a lower mean collision rate and less variability relative to that developed for golden eagles. We determined that the prior probability distributions specific to bald eagles from these operating facilities are a better starting point for predicting take for bald eagles at operating wind energy facilities in an agricultural landscape than those developed for golden eagles. © 2021 The Wildlife Society.

## Research Article

## Predicting Bald Eagle Collision at Wind Energy Facilities

KRISTEN NASMAN,[1] Western EcoSystems Technology, 2121 Midpoint Drive, Suite 201, Fort Collins, CO 80525, USA KIMBERLY BAY, Western EcoSystems Technology, 415 West 17th Street, Suite 200, Cheyenne, WY 82001, USA TODD MATTSON, Western EcoSystems Technology, 7575 Golden Valley Road, Suite 300, Golden Valley, MN 55427, USA JESSE LECKBAND, MidAmerican Energy Company, 666 Grand Avenue, Des Moines, IA 50309, USA DREW BECKER, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 1875 Century Boulevard Northeast, Atlanta, GA 30345, USA

ABSTRACT Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) are currently protected in the United States under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act of 1940 and Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918. Given these protections and the increasing development of wind energy throughout the United States, it is important for regulators and the wind industry to understand the risk of bald eagle collisions with wind turbines. Prior probability distributions for eagle exposure rates and collision rates have been developed for golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). Given similar information has not been available for bald eagles, the current recommendation by the USFWS is to use the prior probability distributions developed using data collected on golden eagles to predict take for bald eagles. But some evidence suggests that bald and golden eagles may be at different risk for collision with wind turbines and the prior probability distributions developed for golden eagles may not be appropriate for bald eagles. We developed prior probability distributions using data collected at MidAmerican Energy Company's operating wind energy facilities in Iowa, USA, from December 2014 to March 2017 for bald eagle exposure rates and collision rates. The prior probability distribution for collision rate developed for bald eagles has a lower mean collision rate and less variability relative to that developed for golden eagles. We determined that the prior probability distributions specific to bald eagles from these operating facilities are a better starting point for predicting take for bald eagles at operating wind energy facilities in an agricultural landscape than those developed for golden eagles. © 2021 The Wildlife Society.

KEY WORDS bald eagle, collision risk model, fatality prediction, Haliaeetus leucocephalus, wind energy.

The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), a species protected in the United States under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act of 1940 and Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918, is broadly distributed across varied landscapes throughout North America (Buehler 2020). With continued expansion of the wind energy industry, there is growing interest in better understanding bald eagle risk for wind turbine collisions. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) published a collision risk model (CRM) in its Eagle Conservation Plan Guidance (ECPG; USFWS 2013) that uses a Bayesian approach to predict annual eagle fatality rates at wind energy facilities. This approach uses statistical models to define the relationship between eagle exposure, collision rate, and fatalities, and accounts for uncertainty (USFWS 2013). New et al. (2015) presented an update to the exposure rate prior probability distribution for golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) defined in the ECPG and stated that the CRM framework could be applied to other avian species, including bald eagles.

The USFWS developed prior probability distributions for the CRM using data collected on golden eagle use and fatalities at wind energy facilities. The exposure rate prior probability distribution was developed using data under USFWS review collected prior to 2013 and the collision rate prior probability distribution was developed using data collected at 4 wind energy facilities in California and Wyoming, USA, with older turbine technology (turbines with a nameplate generating capacity ≤0.75 megawatts; Whitfield 2009). The current recommendation from the USFWS is to use the prior probability distributions developed using data collected on golden eagles to predict take of bald eagles because these distributions have not been developed for bald eagles. The prior probability distributions developed for golden eagles may not be appropriate for bald eagles because evidence suggests that bald eagles may have different risks to wind turbine collisions than golden eagles. Pagel et al. (2013) reported, of the known eagle fatalities reported from wind farms, 79 of these were from golden eagles (92.9%) and 6 were bald eagles (7.1%), despite bald eagles having a significantly larger population and broader distribution (USFWS 2016a).

To help improve predictions of bald eagle fatality rates at wind farms, we developed prior probability distributions

Figure 1. Location of MidAmerican Energy Company wind energy facilities in Iowa, USA, where we conducted bald eagle fatality monitoring studies from 4 December 2014–15 March 2017, and bald eagle use surveys from 4 December 2014–15 March 2016.

using data collected on bald eagles from 18 utility‐scale wind energy facilities in Iowa, USA, collected post‐ construction. The pairing of bald eagle use data collected post‐construction and fatality monitoring data allowed for the development of prior probability distributions for exposure rate and collision rate specific to bald eagles. We used these distributions specific to bald eagles to predict fatality rates as a result of collision with wind turbines.

## STUDY AREA

The study consisted of 18 wind energy facilities (Fig. 1) – ranging in size from 2,821 22,120ha, totaling 156,107 ha for all facilities combined (Table 1) with a generating capacity of 3,496 megawatts. We conducted the study from December 2014 to March 2017. The wind energy facilities were located across Iowa in Des Moines Lobe, Iowan Surface, Loess Hills, Northwest Iowa Plains, and Southern Iowa Drift Plain ecoregions. The topography at the facilities generally consisted of gentle rolling plains with steeper hills at the facilities in the northeastern part of the state. Elevation for these facilities ranged from 280–476 m (Table 1).

According to the National Land Cover Database (Yang et al. 2018, Multi‐Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium 2019), land cover at the facilities (except the Rolling Hills and Macksburg facilities) consisted predominately of cropland (i.e., corn and soybeans). The land cover

at the Rolling Hills and Macksburg facilities was a combination of cropland, pasture, and hay.

Bald eagles are part of the dominant fauna of Iowa (defined as the most relatively abundant species), which

include species that use the native grassland, forested areas, river systems, other aquatic ecosystems, and the predominant agricultural landscape. Other dominant animals in Iowa include game species such as white‐tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), ring‐necked pheasant (Phasianus colchicus), ducks (e.g., mallard [Anas platyrhynchos] and blue‐winged teal [Anas discors]), and Canada goose (Branta canadensis), and fur‐ bearing mammals (e.g., coyote [Canis latrans], red fox [Vulpes vulpes], raccoon [Procyon lotor], skunk [Mephitis mephitis], eastern cottontail [Sylvilagus floridanus], white‐ tailed hare [Lepus townsendii], and muskrat [Ondatra zibethicus]; Iowa Department of Natural Resources 2019). Other dominant bird species include blackbirds, meadowlark species, and American robin (Turdus migratorius), and raptors such as red‐tailed hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) and American kestrel (Falco sparverius). Amphibians and reptiles such as chorus frog (Pseudacris spp.) and garter snake (Thamnophis spp.) are also present.

The surveys covered each of Iowa's 4 seasons, spring (16 Mar–15 May), summer (16 May–31 Jul), fall (1 Aug– 15 Nov), and winter (16 Nov–15 Mar) and the varying weather conditions across the facilities. The coldest month of the year was January with average temperatures in the western part of the state ranging between 1.1°C and 15°C, central Iowa temperatures ranged from 0–13.9°C and the eastern part of the state ranged from 1.1–15°C. Summers were hot and humid where average summer temperatures ranged from 25.6–29.4°C. During the study, the average annual temperature was 9.6°C, which was normal and precipitation was 109.9 cm and 20.3 cm above normal (Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship [IDALS] 2015) in 2014 and in 2015 the average temperature was 10.3°C, which was normal and precipitation totaled 98.5 cm, which was 8.9 inches above normal (IDALS 2015).

## METHODS

We conducted bald eagle use and fatality monitoring surveys from December 2014–March 2017, at each of the 18 MidAmerican Energy Company's operating wind energy facilities in Iowa. We monitored each facility for 15 months. We conducted bald eagle use surveys to estimate eagle exposure rates and fatality monitoring surveys to estimate fatality rates at each facility. We used the estimates of bald eagle use to develop prior probability distributions for exposure rate, and estimates of bald eagle use and fatality rates to develop prior probability distributions for collision rate. We modeled the predicted annual fatality rate in a Bayesian framework and assumed a relationship between bald eagle exposure, collision rate, and fatalities (USFWS 2013).

## Field Methods

We followed proper protocol for animal use and care for all data collection using our established procedure for minimizing disturbance from our personnel on wildlife (Applied Research Ethics National Association 2002). We developed data collection methods based on the voluntary guidelines

developed by the USFWS (Strickland et al. 2011 as cited by USFWS 2012, 2013).

We conducted bald eagle use surveys and fatality monitoring surveys including standard carcass searches, carcass persistent trials, and searcher efficiency trials.

Eagle use surveys.—These surveys provided estimates of bald eagle exposure to wind turbines. We conducted eagle use surveys from 4 December 2014 to 15 March 2016. We defined the study area for the eagle use surveys as the 1‐km buffer around the turbine locations within the facilities based on the survey area defined in the ECPG (USFWS 2013). To assess eagle use, we selected plots to cover ≥30% of the study area (USFWS 2016b). For this study, each facility had ≥10 plots. We combined the area from the Adair and Morning Light facilities and Vienna I and Vienna II facilities for the purposes of calculating percent coverage, total survey hours, and eagle use because the project boundaries of these facilities abutted one another.

– We also conducted surveys in reference areas (801 7,000 m away from operating wind turbines) from 1 November 2014 to 15 March 2015 and from 1 August 2015 to 15 March 2016 to compare the level of bald eagle use in both settings. We selected plots for the reference surveys outside the facilities' boundaries yet adjacent to the wind facilities. To the extent practicable, the number of reference plots equaled the number of plots within the study area for each facility. In an attempt to control for landscape features, we chose reference plots located in similar land cover types and distances from major features such as lakes or rivers as those plots located within the study area.

We designed this survey approach to be consistent with the recommendations included in USFWS's ECPG (USFWS 2013). We conducted surveys in the established study and reference areas within circular plots with an 800‐m radius from the central observation points (fixed points) following methods similar to Reynolds et al. (1980); deviations from these methods are outlined below. Each plot covered approximately 2 km[2] . We developed a pre‐ established schedule prior to the field surveys to ensure that we surveyed each plot approximately the same number of times, to spread survey times throughout the daylight hours, and to minimize travel time between plots. We surveyed each plot for 60 minutes each month using binoculars following the recommend survey effort and coverage outlined in the ECPG. For each plot surveyed, we recorded the survey date, start and end time of the survey, observer, and weather data including temperature, wind speed, wind direction, precipitation, and cloud cover. When we observed an eagle, we recorded the approximate flight height at first observation to the nearest 5 m and the approximate lowest and highest flight heights observed, eagle behavior at first observation, and approximate distance from observer at the first observation and when closest to the observer. Biologists were trained to evaluate distance using topographic maps or satellite imagery and flight heights using features on the landscape with known locations and heights. For each 1‐minute interval the eagle was in view, we recorded eagle

behavior, distance from observer, and flight height (to the nearest 5 m per the ECPG; USFWS 2013).

Fatality monitoring surveys.—We used 3 field components during fatality monitoring surveys including standardized carcass searches, carcass persistence trials, and searcher efficiency trials. We defined the search area for fatality monitoring surveys as a 100‐m buffer around all turbines at each facility and accounted for fatalities that fell outside of the search plots using an area correction. Given the logistics of completing fatality monitoring surveys at all 18 wind facilities, we broke the fatality monitoring surveys into 2 periods. We conducted surveys at the first set of 9 facilities from 4 December 2014 to 15 May 2015, and 16 November 2015 to 15 Mar 2016 and we conducted surveys at the second set of 9 facilities from 16 November 2015 to 15 May 2016, and 16 November 2016 to15 March 2017. We used the data collected from all 18 facilities to estimate bald eagle fatalities for the prior probability distribution for collision rate.

We designed carcass searches specifically to detect eagle carcasses, which we conducted once every 4 weeks during the first winter and every 2 weeks thereafter. Prior to 22 April 2015, we conducted carcass searches at all turbines in winter and spring using 3 methods: searching 70% of turbines using visual scans, searching 15% of turbines using transects 20 m apart, and searching 15% of turbines using transects 40 m apart.

Searchers conducted visual scans within the search area by first scanning the turbine pad and then standing at the edge of the graveled turbine pad at each of the cardinal directions and scanning for eagle carcasses using binoculars. Searchers also conducted carcass searches using transects within 200‐ by 200‐m square plots centered on the turbine. Searchers walked transects placed either 40 m or 20 m apart while scanning the area on both sides of the transect for eagle carcasses. Following our analysis of searcher efficiency data collected at the first set of 9 facilities from December 2014 to April 2015, we confirmed that visual scans were as effective as the transect surveys; therefore, after 22 April 2015, we conducted all remaining searches using visual scans.

We used carcass persistence trials to estimate the average length of time a carcass remained in the search area before being removed by scavengers or by other means. We used estimates of carcass persistence to adjust the number of carcasses found for those removed from the search area prior to a carcass search, thereby correcting for removal bias. We conducted carcass persistence trials approximately monthly to cover changes in weather and the effects of scavengers.

Surrogates for eagle carcasses used in carcass persistence trials were provided by USFWS and included species such ‐ ‐ as Cooper's hawk (Accipiter cooperii), red tailed hawk, short eared owl (Asio flammeus), snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus), sharp‐shinned hawk (Accipiter striatus), and turkey vulture (Cathartes aura). Prior to conducting carcass persistence trials, we marked each trial carcass discreetly with a black zip‐tie around the leg to identify it as a trial carcass. Then, personnel conducting carcass searches dropped the trial carcasses from shoulder height and allowed them to land in a natural posture to simulate a true turbine‐related fatality

within the search areas. Personnel conducting carcass searches monitored the trial carcasses over 60 days by checking them every day for the first 4 days, then on day 7, day 10, day 14, day 20, day 30, day 40, day 50, and day 60. We followed this schedule as closely as possible, but the schedule occasionally varied depending on weather and coordination with other survey work.

We used searcher efficiency trials to estimate the probability that a carcass was found by searchers. We conducted trials within the search area concurrently with carcass searches and used them to adjust the number of carcasses found for carcasses missed by searchers, thereby correcting for detection bias. We conducted searcher efficiency trails across the survey period to provide measurements of searcher efficiency in varying field conditions.

Surrogates for eagle carcasses used for searcher efficiency trials were fully feathered wild turkey decoys and red‐tailed hawk carcasses. We placed carcasses for searcher efficiency trials (trial carcasses) at random locations within the search area prior to scheduled carcass searches for that day. We did not inform searchers when we were conducting searcher efficiency trials, or where we placed trial carcasses. The searchers recorded the number and location of the trial carcasses found during the carcass searches. Personnel responsible for distributing the trial carcasses determined the number of trial carcasses available for detection during each trial immediately after completion of the trial.

We defined the collision rate ( _C_ ) as the rate that an eagle could collide with a turbine per exposure in the hazardous area, where all collisions are considered fatal. The prior probability distribution for collision rate is a Beta distribution and is given as:

where v and v′ are positive shape parameters.

We used a method of moments approach to estimate the parameters for the Beta distribution and we estimated the number of exposure events for each facility by estimating the exposure rate from eagle use survey data collected at each respective facility. We then estimated the expansion factor for each facility using the number of daylight hours during the fatality monitoring study period, rotor radius, and number of turbines at the facility. The product of the exposure rate and the expansion factor during fatality monitoring estimates the number of bald eagle exposures within the hazardous area during fatality monitoring.

## Estimates of Bald Eagle Fatalities

Using the evidence of absence (EoA) framework (Dalthorp et al. 2017), we estimated the number of bald eagle fatalities at each facility (M*) as the minimum number of bald eagle fatalities, such that probability (M < M*) = 0.5, where M is the known number of bald eagle fatalities. To obtain M*, we adjusted the number of bald eagle fatalities found during post‐construction fatality monitoring surveys based on the site‐wide probability that a carcass was available to be found and detected by searchers using carcass persistence rates, searcher efficiency, and area correction for bald eagles.

We estimated the average probability of persistence of a ˆ carcass through the search interval ( _r_ ) from an interval‐ censored survival regression (Kalbfleisch and Prentice 2002, Huso 2011). If the time between searches exceeded the amount of time we expected a carcass to persist, we used an effective search interval that Huso (2011) defined as the length of time beyond which the probability a carcass persists is ≤1%. We fit exponential, log‐logistic, lognormal, and Weibull distributions to data collected on carcass persistence and selected the best model using corrected Akaike's Information Criterion (AICc; Burnham and Anderson 2002). The best model was the most parsimonious model within 2 AICc units of the model with the lowest AICc value. Carcass persistence rates were the estimated average probability that a bald eagle carcass would remain in the study area and be available for detection within the search interval.

We estimated searcher efficiency using a logistic regression model (Agresti 2007). Logistic regression modeled the natural logarithm of the estimated odds of finding an available carcass on the first search. Searcher efficiency was the probability searchers would find a carcass given that the carcass was available to be found.

We estimated an area correction to account for areas where eagles were not viewable from the turbine pads during the

visual scan searches because of obstructions and the area outside of the 100‐m‐radius search plot. We used Hull and Muir's (2013) physics‐based model to predict the maximum fall distance of a carcass for a given turbine height and rotor diameter. We assumed the relative carcass density followed a linear decrease from the turbine base out to the maximum predicted fall distance of a carcass (Huso and Dalthorp 2014). We estimated the proportion of area searched as the amount of area searched divided by the total area for 1‐m annuli around the turbine. To calculate an estimate for area correction, we took the product of the carcass‐density distribution and the proportion of the area searched at each 1‐m annulus and summed across the distances.

## Model Validation

We used leave‐one‐out cross‐validation (Allen 1974) to determine how accurately the prior probability distributions performed when we applied site‐specific data to the CRM. To determine how well the predictions fit the data, we compared the model predictions using the prior probability distributions for exposure rate and collision rate to the estimated fatality rates from fatality monitoring surveys using EoA.

To evaluate the performance of the prior probability distributions, we obtained an independent prediction of annual fatality rate for facility i by omitting the ith facility from the data set. Then, we estimated the parameters for the prior probability distribution for collision rate and exposure rate using the methods described above using the remaining n − 1 facilities, where n is the number of facilities. We used the prior probability distributions for the collision rate and exposure rate to predict annual fatalities for the ith facility. We repeated this process n times to obtain a fatality prediction for each facility. For each facility, we also used the prior probability distributions presented in the ECPG to predict annual bald eagle fatalities.

We used the deviation between the fatality prediction and the estimated number of eagle fatalities from fatality monitoring and the root mean squared prediction error as goodness‐of‐fit metrics to evaluate the fit of the prior probability distributions for exposure rate and collision rate. We placed 76 trial carcasses for the carcass persistence study and monitored the carcasses for 60 days or until removed. We collected and pooled the data during carcass persistence trials across all facilities. The probability a carcass persisted through the search interval was 0.88 and 0.78 for a 14‐ and 28‐day search interval, respectively.

To estimate searcher efficiency, we placed 561 trial decoys or carcass surrogates during fatality monitoring. We fit logistic regression models for each search area and detection rates ranged from 0.50 to 1.00 across the search areas (Table 4).

The calculations for the area correction estimated the proportion of carcasses visible to searchers during visual scans. We estimated the area correction for each facility and the values ranged from 0.75 to 0.95 (Table 4).

We found 3 bald eagle carcasses during fatality monitoring and we included these fatalities in the EoA estimates.

We found single carcasses at the Carroll, Highland, and Macksburg facilities within the search areas during the study period. We found an additional 2 carcasses either outside the search area or after the study period: 1 at the Charles City facility and 1 at the Highland facility. We did not include these carcasses in the EoA estimates.

The overall probability that a bald eagle carcass was both available to be found and detected at a facility during monitoring was <1.00, given carcasses removed by scavengers, imperfect searcher detection rates, and bald eagles that may have fallen outside of the visible areas during scans. The site‐wide probability a carcass was available to be found and detected by searchers ranged from 0.42 to 0.78 across the search areas. Using the EoA framework and the 3 fatalities found in search areas during fatality monitoring, we estimated that 7 bald eagle fatalities would occur at the 18 facilities during the fatality monitoring study.

## DISCUSSION

Based on these study results, the prior probability distributions developed using bald eagle‐specific data offer a more precise starting point for predicting take for bald eagles at operating facilities in an agricultural landscape in Iowa than the prior probability distributions presented in the ECPG and are likely applicable in states surrounding Iowa. The prior probability distributions presented in the ECPG were originally developed using data collected on golden eagles from projects under USFWS review and 4 older wind energy facilities (Whitfield 2009). These older facilities included different turbine sizes and technologies than modern facilities, and the older turbines may have different collision risk than modern turbines (ICF International 2015).

Researchers can make refinements and improvements to avian impact prediction tools as additional information becomes available. In accordance with the ECPG and New et al. (2015), we created new prior probability distributions for exposure rate and collision rate for bald eagles at wind energy facilities in the Bayesian CRM framework. The model validation exercise suggests that the prior probability distributions developed using data collected on bald eagles are more accurate for predicting bald eagle take at wind energy projects in agricultural landscapes relative to those presented in the ECPG (Fig. 5). The key difference between the predictions was that the magnitude of the deviations tended to be more conservative for prior probability distributions presented in the ECPG (i.e., take predictions were higher than the estimated take from post‐construction fatality monitoring studies). Although bald eagles may feed on a variety of prey items, fish can be a dominant food source (Buehler 2020); golden eagles also feed on a variety of prey items, but they rely more heavily on terrestrial mammals such as rabbits and ground squirrels (Katzner et al. 2020). Additionally, landscapes dominated by cultivated agricultural lands such as those found in the study area may also provide different foraging opportunities compared to the grassland or shrub‐ steppe landscapes of the western United States. That is, more limited or poor‐quality foraging areas may result in eagles flying farther and more broadly traveling across the landscape (Krone and Treu 2018). Differences in species ecology or the

landscape composition, or these factors working in combination, may in turn result in differences in exposure and risk of collision with wind turbines.

An underlying assumption of the CRM is that a relationship exists between eagle use (i.e., exposure) and fatalities. The relatively limited data collected during this study do not show a clear correlation between exposure and fatalities (e.g., 2 of the 3 eagle fatalities recorded during this study were from sites with relatively low eagle exposure and comparatively low predicted fatality rates), perhaps not unexpectedly given the relatively low number of eagle fatalities found during fatality monitoring. Other factors may contribute to bald eagle collisions with wind turbines beyond general exposure. For example, bald eagle use might be less predictive of collisions than specific types of eagle use

Although the updated prior probability distributions presented here may be an improvement over existing distributions used in the CRM, additional factors may need to be incorporated as covariates to help further improve the accuracy of bald eagle take predictions.

The new bald eagle‐specific prior probability distributions developed as part of this study can be used to predict collision risk at operating or newly repowered wind projects, or with data collected prior to construction of a facility. Diurnal raptors appear to detect and avoid operating wind turbines to a degree (Garvin et al. 2010, Ferrer et al. 2011, Johnston et al. 2014). This appears also to be true for bald eagles observed near the MidAmerican Energy Company's wind energy facilities included in this study. In comparing the use between surveys conducted near turbines to surveys conducted at reference sites away from turbines over the same periods, bald eagle use was about 25% lower near turbines compared to the reference points away from turbines (Table 3). This reduction in exposure suggests that the use of pre‐construction eagle use survey data with the updated bald eagle‐specific prior probability distributions in the CRM framework could likely result in conservative predictions of fatality rates because actual bald eagle use, and thus exposure, would likely decrease at an operating wind farm compared to eagle use prior to the presence of wind turbines. The updated bald eagle‐specific prior probability distributions presented here are expected to result in take predictions that are 5 to 7 times lower than what would be shown by the CRM when using the prior probability distributions included in the ECPG.

The Bayesian framework for the CRM presented in the ECPG allows incorporation of new information as it becomes available to improve predictions of eagle fatalities. Using bald eagle‐specific prior probability distributions developed from studies such as this is an appropriate way to incorporate new information into the Bayesian framework, and allows wind operators and regulators to better understand risk and improve management decisions related to bald eagles. Additional methods could be developed to allow practitioners to use pre‐construction use data with a bald eagle‐specific prior probability distribution for collision rate that was developed with data collected post‐construction. Future research should involve using the study data collected both near and away from turbines to develop an adjustment that could be applied to account for the difference in bald eagle use pre‐and post‐construction.

## MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS

Development and use of prior probability distributions based on bald eagle exposure data collected near operating wind turbines has important implications for the wind industry. The prior probability distributions presented in the ECPG uses eagle use data gathered prior to facility construction to predict eagle fatalities once facilities are op‐ erational. Adequate pre construction eagle use data may not be available for all wind energy facilities, particularly if the facility was placed in service prior to the release of the ECPG in 2013. We collected data on bald eagle use as part of this study while turbines were operating and used this data to predict eagle fatality risk for the operating turbines. The resulting prior probability distributions developed as part of this study are best suited for use in a CRM framework for facilities that have also collected post‐construction bald eagle use data in an agricultural landscape in or near

Iowa. Bald eagle use data collected near operating turbines may also be used in predicting risk at repowered turbines. Because repowered turbines remain in the same location as previous turbines, there is no meaningful opportunity to collect eagle use data without operational turbines present. The updated prior probability distributions for exposure rate and collision rate presented in this study can provide a more accurate take prediction for bald eagle fatalities at facilities where bald eagle use data are collected post‐construction, including repowered facilities in an agricultural landscape in or near Iowa. The take predictions using the updated prior probability distributions, regardless of the lack of correlation between bald eagle use and bald eagle fatalities, were within the magnitude of the observed take for this study and also provide more accurate take predictions compared to the take predictions developed using the prior distributions developed for golden eagles by the USFWS in the CRM. Additionally, there may be applications for the prior probability distributions developed when bald eagle use data are collected pre‐construction.
